2.title: Why a clinical bottleneck?
detailed: Let's start with a simple question. Why is traditional sleep medicine stuck in a bottleneck?
Look at this cycle, between the patient, the physician, and the hospital.
First, the data are fragmented. Usually, we get a single-night snapshot.
Second, we depend heavily on the hospital, which means a lot of medical resources and physical bed space.
Third, it's inconvenient for patients. They have to come in just so we can collect data.
And finally, there are treatment blind spots.
Once patients go home, it's hard to know whether our treatment is actually being used, or whether it's working.

It's inconvenient for patients.
And after they go home, we don't know if the treatment works.

3.title: Evaluating existing detection methods
detailed: So, how do the existing methods compare?
Polysomnography covers all sleep disorders, but it needs twenty or more wires, and the wait can be one to two months.
Home sleep testing is OSA-specific. It uses three wires, and it takes about a week.
A finger oximeter or a chest ECG patch can start right away and record for seven to fourteen days.
But they're uncomfortable, and patches often cause skin allergy.
So, none of these options gives us comfortable, multi-night monitoring.
That gap is exactly why we need to move from wearables to completely non-wearable, continuous monitoring.

6.title: Radar principle diagram
detailed: Our answer is a 24-gigahertz continuous-wave radar.
On the left, you can see the unit on the wall above a ward bed, at a distance, D-zero, from the user.
The antennas send out a 24-gigahertz signal and pick up the reflection from the chest wall, without a single wire.
A tiny chest movement, delta-x, changes the received signal compared with the one we sent.
That shows up as time of flight, and as a phase shift, delta-phi.
From these tiny changes, we rebuild the breathing signal, and the analysis runs on deep neural decision trees.
concise: Our answer is a 24-gigahertz radar on the wall.
It sends a signal and picks up the reflection from the chest.
Tiny chest movements change the phase of the signal.
From these changes, we rebuild the breathing, with no wires.

8.title: Three-phase technical roadmap
detailed: Our work followed a three-phase roadmap, from the sleep lab to cardiology.
All of it is built on 24-gigahertz continuous-wave radar, combined with deep neural decision trees.
Phase one, clinical purity. 196 patients, compared directly with gold-standard polysomnography, with a correlation of r equals 0.91.
Phase two, real-world utility. 80 patients, and 147 nights of home sleep assessment, with no professional setup.
Phase three, cross-domain translation. In 72 patients, radar-captured periodic breathing was associated with impaired left ventricular ejection fraction.
Let me walk you through each phase.
concise: Our work had three phases.
First, the hospital. 196 patients, with a correlation of 0.91.
Second, the home. 80 patients over 147 nights.
Third, the heart. In 72 patients, periodic breathing was associated with lower heart function.

11.title: Airflow defines the event; radar sees the chest wall
detailed: In the sleep lab, an apnea or a hypopnea is defined by airflow.
After normal breathing, airflow stops, or becomes shallow, and we can only see that when we actually measure airflow.
A radar does something different. It senses the rise and fall of the chest wall, not airflow.
And that creates blind spots.
In an obstructive event, the airway is closed, but the patient keeps trying to breathe, so the chest keeps moving, even though no air is flowing.
Chest motion is not the same as airflow.
So the radar can't just look for a flat line. It has to recognize a characteristic sequence of chest-motion changes.
concise: In the sleep lab, events are defined by airflow.
The radar doesn't see airflow. It sees the chest moving.
When the airway is blocked, the chest still moves.
So the radar must look for a pattern, not a flat line.

12.title: The radar-detectable sleep-breathing event
detailed: So, what does the radar actually look for? A five-phase sequence.
One. Normal chest movement, at normal amplitude.
Two. At apnea onset, the amplitude drops sharply, or stops completely.
Three. The airway's still closed, but the chest starts to struggle, so we see small up-and-down movements from the effort to breathe.
Four. When the airway finally opens, there's one big surge, the recovery breath.
And five. Breathing goes back to its normal amplitude.
It's this whole pattern, not a single drop, that defines a sleep-breathing event the radar can detect.
And please note, this waveform is a schematic, not patient data.
concise: Here's the pattern, in five steps.
Normal breathing.
Then the movement drops or stops.
Then small struggling movements, while the airway is closed.
Then one big recovery breath.
Then back to normal.
This picture is a schematic.

In our validation data from 196 patients, the correlation between the two was r equals 0.91.
That's very strong agreement, and nothing ever touches the patient.

14.title: Act I: Hospital accuracy & results
detailed: Let's look at the hospital results in more detail.
The scatter plot compares the radar's bRDI with the PSG AHI. The correlation is r equals 0.91, with p less than 0.01.
For moderate-to-severe OSA, accuracy was 90.3 percent, at a cut-off of 19.2 events per hour.
For severe OSA, accuracy was 92.4 percent, at a cut-off of 28.86 events per hour.
And for four-class prediction, normal, mild, moderate and severe, the average accuracy was 83.7 percent.

15.title: From validation to the ward (SNQ 2021 / NHQA 2022)
detailed: Now, validation only matters if it reaches patients.
So we took the radar into routine inpatient care, as a zero-contact care platform.
It monitors breathing continuously, tracks heart rate from the same radar signal, and records whether the patient is in bed or out of bed.

Alerts go straight to the care team. A reminder when a patient's been out of bed too long, flags for abnormal vital signs on the ward dashboard, and push notifications through the dashboard and LINE Notify.
This platform received the 2021 SNQ, the Symbol of National Quality, and our sleep center received the 2022 NHQA Distinctive Center award.

Overall, 138 of 147 nights, or 93.88 percent, fell within the plus-or-minus 1.96 SD limits of agreement.
And I want to stress this. These are limits of agreement, not a confidence interval.

31.title: Why does cardiac impairment alter breathing?
detailed: So, why would a weak heart change breathing during sleep?
This loop shows the main parts of breathing control. Neural outflow, plant gain, which is the change in PCO2 for a change in ventilation, circulation time, and chemoreflex gain to CO2.
The heart enters this loop through circulation time.
That's why periodic breathing is associated with impaired cardiac function.
And just to be clear, the radar doesn't measure CO2. It only sees the breathing pattern that results.
concise: Why does a weak heart change breathing?
Breathing is controlled by a feedback loop, and a weak heart slows circulation.
So periodic breathing is associated with impaired heart function.
The radar doesn't measure CO2. It only sees the breathing pattern.

32.title: Periodic-breathing features & cycle length
detailed: Periodic breathing has features we can measure. Cycle length, apnea-hypopnea length, hyperpnea length, hyperpnea shape, and the hyperpnea initial jump, as described for ApneaLink in SLEEP, 2009.
Cycle length is especially interesting.
In data from Wedewardt and colleagues, cycle length gets longer as LVEF falls, from about 49 seconds with an LVEF above 50 percent, to about 86 seconds below 20 percent.
And for CPAP-measured cycle length, the ratio was eleven times in acute heart failure, and eight times in chronic heart failure, compared with one times in normal hearts.

Cycle length is the most interesting.
In published data, the cycle gets longer as heart function falls, from about 49 to about 86 seconds.

Age, sex, BMI, and comorbidity scores were similar, while LVEF, LVEDD and LVESD were significantly different.

34.title: Quantifying the cardiopulmonary associations
detailed: Then we quantified these relationships, and again, they're clinical associations only.
For each one-event-per-hour increase in RDI, LVEF was 0.22 percent lower, and LVESD was 0.14 millimeters larger.

For each one-second increase in periodic-breathing cycle length, NT-proBNP was 158.49 picograms per milliliter higher, LVEF was 0.21 percent lower, LVEDD was 0.11 millimeters larger, and LVESD was 0.16 millimeters larger.
concise: These are associations only.
A higher RDI went with a lower ejection fraction.
A longer cycle went with a higher NT-proBNP.

38.title: Take-home messages
detailed: Let me close with five take-home messages.
One. 24-gigahertz contactless radar gives us continuous, multi-night monitoring, with no burden on the patient.
Two. Accuracy held up both in the controlled hospital setting, with an r of 0.91, and in unattended homes, with an r of 0.87.
Three. It works as a TFDA-cleared screen for suspected severe OSA, at a bRDI of 30 or more, with 90.5 percent sensitivity.
Four. Ongoing research shows associations between periodic breathing and cardiac impairment.
And five. This work has been recognized with the SNQ in 2021, and NHQA awards in 2022 and 2025.
Thank you very much for your attention. I'm happy to take your questions.
